## Script (verbatim, labelled)

[VILLAIN] [MONEY]
[0:00] The most expensive thing an HVAC tech will ever try to sell you is a thousand-dollar box that bolts into your ductwork to clean your air.

[POINT]
[0:09] But the sales pitch leaves out what's actually inside it. That box works by making hydrogen peroxide, the same thing in the one-dollar brown bottle under your sink.

[PROMISE]
[0:19] Once you know that, you start seeing how much of your HVAC bill a dollar bottle already covers.

[PROMISE] [MOTIVE: banned]
[0:24] There are 11 of them, and number five is the one the whole industry would rather you never notice.

[ITEM] (1)
[0:32] Number one, and this is why half the people who try this swear it doesn't work. The bottle of peroxide already under your sink is probably dead.

[MECHANISM]
[0:40] Hydrogen peroxide is water with one extra oxygen atom, and that atom is always trying to escape. Light, heat, and air all speed it up. So a bottle that's been sitting open in a warm cabinet for eight months has turned into plain water. People pour it in, nothing happens, and they decide the whole thing is a myth. It isn't. Their peroxide just expired.

[CHECK]
[1:02] Here's the test. Pour a little on something dirty, a grease spot, a bit of mildew, anything organic. If it fizzes, it's alive, and it works. If it just sits there flat, it's done.

[ITEM] (1, cont.)
[1:17] That's why it comes in a brown bottle in the first place. The dark plastic slows the light from breaking it down. Buy a fresh one, keep the cap on tight, store it somewhere dark, and replace it once a year. That fizz is the entire point of everything that follows. So start with a bottle that still has one.

[ITEM] (2) [SAFETY]
[1:38] Number two, the number on the label that matters, and the trap of thinking bigger is better. The brown bottle is 3%. It's strong enough to tear apart mold, algae, and bacteria, and gentle enough that it won't hurt you or your equipment. The internet will tell you to grab the 6% or the food grade 35% because if a little works, more must work better. Don't. Food grade peroxide at 35% is a corrosive chemical that burns skin on contact and can damage the plastic and metal parts inside your system.

[2:14] The 3% bottle is already the right strength, dialed in on purpose to clean without doing damage. Everything in this video uses that same 3% straight from the bottle, no mixing, no diluting. If a fix ever seems slow, that means your peroxide has gone flat and you just need a fresher bottle.

[ITEM] (3)
[2:35] Number three, the clog that shuts your whole system down in July. Your AC pulls gallons of water a day out of the air and all of it drains through one white PVC pipe. Inside that pipe, it's dark, damp, and warm. So, algae and mold grow a slimy film on the wall. The film grabs dust and eventually the pipe packs solid. When it blocks, a float switch trips and shuts the whole system off on purpose so the water doesn't back up into your ceiling.

[MECHANISM]
[3:06] The unit was never broken. The pipe was dirty.

[ITEM] (3, cont.)
[3:10] Find the T-shaped fitting with a cap on that pipe near your indoor unit, pull the cap and pour in a cup of your fresh 3% peroxide. You'll hear it fizz as it eats the slime and lifts it off the wall. 10 minutes, flush with warm water. Do it once a month through cooling season and that shutdown never comes.

[3:32] If it's already blocked and your system is down, add one step first. Go outside, find where that drain line exits your house, seal a wet dry vacuum over the end of it and run it 2 or 3 minutes to pull the plug out from the far end. Then treat the line with peroxide from inside.

[MONEY]
[3:50] Clearing this on a service call runs you $145 to $245. The bottle and a vacuum you already own do it for about a dollar.

[ITEM] (4) [MONEY]
[4:02] Number four, and this is the money they never bring up because it isn't a repair, it's your electric bill. Everyone talks about the service call. Nobody mentions what a dirty system costs you every single month it runs.

[MECHANISM]
[4:15] That same biological film grows on your evaporator coil, the indoor coil your air blows across to get cold. Once it coats the fins, it works exactly like a blanket over a cold surface. Your air can't touch the cold metal, heat transfer drops, and the system just runs longer and longer to hit the temperature on your thermostat.

[4:35] This isn't a guess. The engineering society ASHRAE puts the efficiency loss from a fouled coil at 10% to 25% and the US Department of Energy says a dirty coil can raise your energy use by as much as 30%. That's up to a third of your cooling bill every month from May to October lost to a layer of slime nobody sees, and it builds up faster than you think. A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study found a typical coil fouls enough to choke its own air flow in about 7.5 years, long before the coil itself wears out.

[UNSAFE: banned]
[5:12] If you can safely reach the coil with the power off at the breaker, mist the fins with 3% peroxide and let it drain into the pan below. Spring is the time to do it before the first hot day so you're not paying that penalty all summer.

[MONEY]
[5:30] That wasted efficiency costs you far more over a season than the repair ever would.

[ITEM] (5) [VILLAIN]
[5:37] Number five, the big one, the $1,000 machine that makes the exact same thing that's in your bottle. At some point, a tech is going to recommend an induct air purifier. The most common one is called a Reme Halo, and there are others, the iWave, the Air Scrubber. It bolts into your ductwork, and here's what the brochure buries in the fine print.

[MECHANISM]
[6:00] It works by generating hydrogen peroxide. The company that makes it, RGF Environmental, calls the process photohydroionization. That's a long way of saying it turns moisture in your air into ionized hydrogen peroxide and blows it through your ducts to kill mold, odors, and bacteria. It is quite literally a machine that manufactures a trace mist of the same molecule sitting in your $1 bottle.

[MONEY]
[6:24] That device runs $600 to $1,000 installed, plus a replacement cell every couple years at $150 to $250.

[SCOPE]
[6:37] Now, I'm going to be fair to it because that matters. The machine does something your bottle can't. It treats the air in your whole house continuously, every room, all day. And the bottle only cleans the wet part you pour it into. So, it's a real product doing real work. It's also, in the words of one HVAC company's own review, one of the most oversold add-ons in the trade. Two things they tend to leave out. It doesn't replace your filter, dust and pollen still need something to physically catch them, and it gives off a small amount of ozone as a byproduct. That's below the EPA's limit for a room you live in, but worth asking about if anyone in the house is sensitive.

[MONEY]
[7:17] If a tech quotes you more than $1,000 for the unit by itself, get a second opinion.

[SCOPE] [CALL A PRO]
[7:23] Just know exactly what you're paying for. You're paying for a machine that makes hydrogen peroxide, and to be straight with you, peroxide is not magic. It kills biological growth, the mold and slime and algae in the wet parts of your system, and that's it. It does nothing for a dead capacitor, low refrigerant, or a bad blower motor. And refrigerant work is licensed for a real reason.

[FORWARD]
[7:50] But that living layer is behind a shocking number of the calls and the upsells you pay for. And the rest of this list is where it hides.

[ITEM] (6)
[7:59] Number six, the outdoor unit that's throwing swamp water on itself. Everyone treats the inside of the system and forgets the big metal box outside. On a lot of units, a slinger ring flings collected condensation straight onto the hot outdoor coil to help it cool. And that standing water goes stagnant with the same algae and mold. On top of that, the outdoor coil sits out in leaves, grass clippings, and dust. And when it fouls, the compressor has to work harder to dump heat, which is more strain and more electricity for the same cooling.

[UNSAFE: banned] [SAFETY]
[8:34] Cut the power at the disconnect. Clear the big debris by hand, then spray 3% peroxide across the coil fins, and the base where water pools. Let it fizz and rinse it gently with a hose from the inside out.

[SAFETY]
[8:48] Don't jam a pressure washer at it. You'll bend the fins flat and make it worse. If some fins are already bent, a cheap fin comb straightens them so air can move through again.

[MONEY]
[9:01] A clean outdoor coil keeps the compressor from grinding all summer to dump the same heat. And a strained compressor is the single most expensive part in the whole system to replace.

[CTA]
[9:14] If this is already changing how you look at your last few HVAC bills, subscribe because we do one of these every week.

[ITEM] (7)
[9:21] Number seven, that musty smell that hits for the first minute every time the AC kicks on. It has a name in the trade. They call it dirty sock syndrome, and it's not the ducts, it's the coil. It's the same biological film from number four growing in the cold wet fins of your evaporator. And every time the blower starts, it pushes that smell out ahead of the cold air.

[UNSAFE: banned]
[9:45] If you can reach the coil safely with the breaker off, spray it down with 3% peroxide, let it sit, let it drain into the pan.

[SCOPE]
[9:54] One honest limit. Peroxide kills the living layer, but it won't dissolve the greasy bonded gunk that also cakes a badly neglected coil. And that needs a real foaming coil cleaner.

[SAFETY]
[10:07] And if your coil is behind a sealed panel, leave it shut. And treat the pan and drain line underneath. Because that's what's feeding the growth anyway.

[ITEM] (8) [MONEY]
[10:17] Number eight, the black spots on your vents. That a company wants to turn into a $900 job. Pull one of your supply registers off the wall or ceiling. The whole thing, not just the grill. Look down into the metal boot behind it. In a humid house, that metal sweats. And where there's moisture and dust, you get black mildew spotting on the inside.

[ITEM] (8, cont.)
[10:40] Spray it with 3% peroxide until it's wet. Give it 10 minutes and wipe it out with a rag on a stick. Wash the grill in the sink at the same time.

[MONEY] [SCOPE]
[10:51] Now the part that saves you real money. Spotting on a boot you can reach with your hand is a surface you can clean yourself in 5 minutes. It is not proof your entire duct system needs a $900 cleaning.

[MOTIVE: banned]
[11:02] And any company quoting you that off a photo of one vent is running a sales call, not an inspection.

[ITEM] (9)
[11:12] Number nine, the one machine in your house that puts whatever's growing in it straight into your lungs. Everything else on this list, the dirty water drains away from you. A humidifier does the opposite. It takes standing water and turns it into a mist you breathe in. So whatever film is growing inside that tank ends up in the air and in you.

[ITEM] (9, cont.)
[11:32] Empty it completely, fill the tank half with 3% peroxide, and half with water, and let it sit 30 minutes. Get the wick housing and the mist nozzle. Rinse it twice and let it air dry before you refill.

[CHECK]
[11:49] A cloudy tank with white scale is your signal it's overdue because that scale is exactly where the growth anchors.

[ITEM] (9, cont.)
[11:56] If you've got a whole house humidifier mounted on the furnace, its water panel gets the same treatment. Though most of those are built to be swapped once a year rather than cleaned. Same idea for a dehumidifier bucket in the basement. Swirl peroxide up the walls and do the float that tells it when to shut off.

[ITEM] (10) [MECHANISM]
[12:16] Number 10. And this is why you can trust a dollar bottle to do a professional job. Hydrogen peroxide isn't some folk remedy someone made up online. In its vapor form, it's a recognized sterilant that hospitals use to decontaminate entire rooms and that food and pharmaceutical plants use to sanitize their equipment. It's the same chemistry that gets called in to wipe down a hospital room after a serious infection, vaporized and sealed in overnight. The reason it works everywhere from an operating room to your AC drain is the same. When it touches something living, it oxidizes it, breaks it apart, and then falls apart itself into nothing but water and oxygen. No toxic residue, no film left behind.

[MONEY]
[13:00] That $1,000 machine from number five is selling you the industrial idea. The brown bottle is the same idea at the strength you actually need for a dollar.

[ITEM] (11) [SAFETY]
[13:12] Number 11. And this one isn't a tip. It's a rule that keeps you safe. Never mix hydrogen peroxide with vinegar. Not in the same container, not one poured right after the other into a line. Together they form parasitic acid and that's not an internet scare story. It's stated plainly in Plumbing and Mechanical, a trade magazine written for HVAC professionals. Peracetic acid is corrosive, and it burns your eyes, your lungs, and your skin. If you insist on using both, the guidance is to dose with peroxide, wait 10 minutes, flush completely with water, and only then use vinegar. That water flush is the entire safety margin. And never use bleach in your system because it eats the cement in your PVC joints and corrodes metal drain pans, which is the exact repair you were trying to avoid. One bottle, 3%, nothing mixed in. That's the whole method.

[END]
[14:11] So, here's the thread through all 11. Peroxide doesn't fix machines. It kills the living layer that makes machines look broken and run expensive in every wet part of your system. And it's the same thing that a $1,000 box makes and that hospitals sterilize with.

- **Coil methods disputed by technicians (labelled unsafe; check against the brief):** [5:12] "If you can safely reach the coil with the power off at the breaker" then [5:17] "mist the fins with 3% peroxide"; [8:36] "spray 3% peroxide across the coil fins"; [9:47] "spray it down with 3% peroxide". About nine HVAC commenters say peroxide corrodes aluminium coils and makers say water only ("Lennox actually says right on their coils to ONLY USE WATER", 31 likes). Never put a method on equipment the brief hasn't cleared.
- **Named products and a named company, with a disputed claim:** [6:00] "It works by generating hydrogen peroxide." and [6:01] "The company that makes it, RGF Environmental, calls the process" (the purifier is also named by brand). Commenters say these units make ozone, not peroxide (about 3). Our rules never state anything negative about a named company as fact, and a claim like this needs the brief.
- **An unattributed quote:** [6:52] "in the words of one HVAC company's own review, one of the most oversold add-ons in the trade". If the brief can't name it, don't quote it.
- **Contradicts itself (my own check):** [2:21] "Everything in this video uses that same 3% straight from the bottle" and [2:23] "no mixing, no diluting", then [11:35] "fill the tank half with 3% peroxide, and half with water".
- **A stretched proof line (my own check):** [12:23] "In its vapor form, it's a recognized sterilant that hospitals use" is offered as why a 3% bottle does a professional job; hospital vapour systems use far stronger peroxide. Check against the brief.
- **Unchecked citations:** [4:38] "The engineering society ASHRAE puts the efficiency loss from a fouled coil"; [5:01] "A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study found a typical coil"; the Plumbing and Mechanical citation at 13:30 (`02-competitors.md`: not checked).
